blocks.prompt: 11. If \(y = a\cos(\ln x) + b\sin(\ln x)\), show that \(x^{2}y_{2} + xy_{1} + y = 0\).
blocks.explanation:
Yahan \(\ln x\) ke andar trig functions hain, is liye har derivative ke saath chain rule ka \(\frac{1}{x}\) aata hai.
Diya kya hai? \(y = a\cos(\ln x) + b\sin(\ln x)\).
Saabit kya karna hai? \(x^{2}y_{2} + xy_{1} + y = 0\).
Rule kaunsa? Chain rule aur product rule.
Plan: \(y_{1}\) nikal kar pehle \(x\) se multiply, phir \(xy_{1}\) ko differentiate, phir dobara \(x\) se multiply.
steps:
Diya gaya: \(y = a\cos(\ln x) + b\sin(\ln x)\) ...(1), \(x > 0\).
Saabit karna: \(x^{2}y_{2} + xy_{1} + y = 0\).
Tareeqa: chain rule mein \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}\). Agar \(y_{1}\) ko seedha differentiate karein to quotient rule lagega; behtar hai pehle \(x\) se multiply kar ke fraction hata dein. Result mein bhi \(xy_{1}\) aur \(x^{2}y_{2}\) hain, yeh is raaste ka ishara hai.

Pehla derivative
\[y_{1} = -\dfrac{a\sin(\ln x)}{x} + \dfrac{b\cos(\ln x)}{x}\]
\[xy_{1} = -a\sin(\ln x) + b\cos(\ln x) \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Kyun: \(\cos(\ln x)\) ka derivative \(-\sin(\ln x)\cdot\frac{1}{x}\), aur \(\sin(\ln x)\) ka \(\cos(\ln x)\cdot\frac{1}{x}\). Phir dono taraf \(x\) se multiply kiya taa ke \(\frac{1}{x}\) khatam ho.

(2) ko differentiate karein
\[xy_{2} + y_{1} = -\dfrac{a\cos(\ln x)}{x} - \dfrac{b\sin(\ln x)}{x}\]
\[xy_{2} + y_{1} = -\dfrac{y}{x}\]
Kyun: left side \(xy_{1}\) do cheezon ka product hai, to product rule: \(x \cdot y_{2} + 1 \cdot y_{1}\). Right side par phir chain rule ka \(\frac{1}{x}\) aaya, aur \(-\frac{1}{x}\) common nikalne par bracket mein asal \(y\) (equation 1) aa gaya.
Dhyan dein: \(xy_{1}\) ka derivative sirf \(xy_{2}\) likh dena (product rule bhool jana) aam ghalti hai.

\(x\) se multiply karein
\[x^{2}y_{2} + xy_{1} = -y\]
\[x^{2}y_{2} + xy_{1} + y = 0\]
Kyun: fraction hatane ke liye dono taraf \(x\) se multiply kiya, phir \(y\) ko left par le aaye. Yahi saabit karna tha.
